messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 74

James is an eighteen-year-old man who sits very still in the chair across from me, his hands folded precisely in his lap. He arrived twenty minutes early for our session, and when I opened the door to the waiting room, he was the only one there, staring at a spot on the wall. He is a tax consultant at a mid-sized firm, a job he started only three months ago. He tells me this with a flat, measured voice, as if reciting a fact from a manual. He is from a small country in West Africa, and he came to the United States alone two years ago on a student visa. He has no family here.

The event happened seven months ago, in the late spring. James was walking home from his night class in accounting. It was a route he had taken dozens of times, a well-lit path through a residential neighborhood near the university. A man came up behind him, pressed something hard and cold into his lower back, and forced him into the narrow space between two parked vans. James tells me this part without pausing, his eyes fixed on a point just above my left shoulder. He describes the smell of the man’s breath, the feel of the gravel digging into his knees, the way the streetlight cast a long, distorted shadow of them both against the side of the van. He does not say the word for what happened. He says, "He did what he did."

In the weeks that followed, James did not tell anyone. He went to his classes. He took his exams. He graduated with a 3.9 GPA. He interviewed for the tax consultant position and was hired. He found an apartment. He bought a suit. He did all of these things as if he were a machine executing a program. He tells me that during this time, he felt nothing. He describes it as a kind of silence, a heavy, muffled quiet in his head where his thoughts used to be.

The silence began to crack about two months ago, when the nightmares started. He doesn't sleep anymore, not really. He lies in bed, rigid, listening to the sounds of his apartment building. A creaking pipe is the click of a weapon. The hum of the refrigerator is a low, threatening voice. He has started sleeping on the floor of his closet, because it is the smallest room in the apartment, and he can press his back against the wall. He says it feels safer, like being in a vault.

At work, he is meticulous, almost painfully so. He checks every line of a tax form three, four, five times. His supervisor has praised his attention to detail, told him he has a "gift for precision." James does not tell her that he is terrified of making a single mistake, because he is convinced that a mistake will lead to a complaint, which will lead to an investigation, which will lead to him being exposed, humiliated, and sent away. He cannot explain why this chain of events feels so real, so inevitable. He just knows that he cannot stop checking.

He has stopped taking the bus. The press of bodies, the warmth of a stranger's arm against his—it makes his skin crawl with a revulsion that is almost physical. He walks to work, a forty-minute commute, taking the longest, most circuitous route possible, even though it takes him through an industrial area that is empty and dark. He tells me that the empty streets feel safer than the crowded bus. He knows this is not logical. He says this often: "I know this is not logical."

He has not touched another person since that night. He flinches when a colleague claps him on the shoulder. He has stopped shaking hands. He sits at his desk with his back to the wall, and he watches the door. He has a small, sharp pocketknife in his briefcase now. He has never used it. He carries it the way someone else might carry a lucky coin.

When I ask him what he feels, he struggles. "I feel like I am waiting," he says, finally. "I am waiting for it to happen again. I am waiting for someone to find out. I am waiting for the real punishment to begin." He looks at me then, and for the first time, his eyes are not flat. They are dark and wide and full of a quiet, exhausted terror. He is waiting.
